notes.definition: Speed is the distance travelled per unit time. It is a scalar quantity (it has no direction) measured in metres per second (m/s), and for constant speed, distance travelled = speed × time.
explanation: Speed tells you how fast an object is moving: how much distance it covers each second. An object moving at 4 m/s travels 4 metres every second. Speed is a scalar quantity because it has a size but no direction. The SI unit is metres per second (m/s), although km/h and miles per hour (mph) are used for vehicles.

For an object moving at a constant speed, distance travelled = speed × time, or s = v t, where s is distance in metres, v is speed in metres per second and t is time in seconds. You must be able to recall this equation and rearrange it: v = s ÷ t and t = s ÷ v. Always convert to SI units first: minutes and hours to seconds, kilometres to metres.

In real life, objects rarely move at a constant speed for a whole journey. A car speeds up, slows down for junctions and stops at traffic lights. A person walking or running changes speed too. For non-uniform motion we calculate the average speed: average speed = total distance travelled ÷ total time taken. This is what the equation s = v t gives you when you use the total distance and total time.

The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on several factors: their age, their fitness, the terrain (for example uphill, rough ground or sand) and the distance they are travelling (people cannot keep up a sprint over long distances). Typical values you should recall are: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s.

You should also know typical speeds for transport. A car in town travels at roughly 13 m/s (about 30 mph) and on a motorway up to about 31 m/s (70 mph). A fast train may travel at about 50 m/s and a passenger aircraft cruises at about 250 m/s. It is not only moving objects whose speed varies: the speed of the wind changes all the time, and the speed of sound in air depends on conditions such as temperature. A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.

To measure the speed of an object you need a distance and a time. In a simple experiment, mark out a measured distance with a tape measure or trundle wheel, and time how long the object takes to cover it with a stopwatch. For more accurate measurements, especially of fast objects or short times, light gates connected to a data logger remove the human reaction time from the timing.
keyFacts: Speed is a scalar quantity: it has magnitude but no direction.
SI unit of speed: metres per second (m/s).
distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t (recall this equation).
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, for non-uniform motion.
Typical walking speed is about 1.5 m/s.
Typical running speed is about 3 m/s.
Typical cycling speed is about 6 m/s.
Typical speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
A person's speed depends on age, fitness, terrain and distance travelled.
Typical car speeds: about 13 m/s in town and up to about 31 m/s on a motorway; aircraft about 250 m/s.
To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 1000 then divide by 3600 (equivalent to dividing by 3.6).

keyTerms.definition: The distance an object travels per unit time. A scalar quantity measured in m/s.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken, used when speed varies during a journey.
Speed that does not change: equal distances are covered in equal times.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as speed, distance or time.
A sensor that records the time when an object breaks an infrared beam, used with a data logger to measure times accurately.
The SI unit of speed: the number of metres travelled in each second.

workedExamples.title: Calculating speed
workedExamples.question: A student runs 100 m in 16 s. Calculate her average speed.
steps: Write the equation: s = v t, so v = s ÷ t.

workedExamples.title: Rearranging and converting minutes to seconds
workedExamples.question: A person walks at 1.5 m/s for 12 minutes. Calculate the distance they walk.
steps: Convert the time to seconds: 12 minutes × 60 = 720 s.

workedExamples.title: Converting km/h to m/s
workedExamples.question: A car travels at 54 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s and calculate the time it takes to travel 450 m.
steps: Rearrange s = v t to t = s ÷ v.

workedExamples.title: Average speed for a journey in two parts
workedExamples.question: A cyclist rides 3.0 km in 10 minutes, then 2.4 km in 5 minutes. Calculate the average speed for the whole journey in m/s.
steps: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 5400 ÷ 900.
Average speed = 6.0 m/s. (Do not average the two separate speeds: the times are different.)

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think speed is a vector because a moving object is always going somewhere.
misconceptions.right: In fact speed has no direction, so it is a scalar. Speed in a given direction is velocity, which is a vector.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think average speed is found by adding the speeds for each part of a journey and dividing by the number of parts.
misconceptions.right: In fact average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Simply averaging speeds only works if each part takes the same time.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often substitute times in minutes or hours, or distances in km, straight into s = v t and give the answer in m/s.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must convert to metres and seconds first (1 min = 60 s, 1 h = 3600 s, 1 km = 1000 m) to get an answer in m/s.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the speed of sound is always exactly the same.
misconceptions.right: In fact the speed of sound varies with the material and conditions (such as air temperature). 330 m/s is a typical value in air.

realWorld: Average speed cameras on motorways time cars between two cameras a known distance apart and calculate average speed = distance ÷ time.
You can estimate how far away a lightning strike is by counting the seconds between seeing the flash and hearing the thunder: every 3 seconds is about 1 km, because sound travels at about 330 m/s.
Fitness apps and sports watches use GPS to measure distance and time, then display running or cycling speed.
Town planners use typical walking speeds (about 1.5 m/s) to set how long pedestrian crossing lights stay green.
examTips: Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit. You can get method marks even if the final answer is wrong.
Check units before substituting: convert km to m (× 1000), minutes to s (× 60) and hours to s (× 3600).
Learn the typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, sound 330 m/s. Questions often ask you to estimate using these.
For average speed, always use total distance ÷ total time, including any time spent stopped.
Sense-check answers: a person walking at 20 m/s or a car at 0.2 m/s means a unit or rearrangement mistake.
summary: Speed is a scalar: distance per unit time, in m/s.
s = v t (recall); rearrange to v = s ÷ t or t = s ÷ v.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time for non-uniform motion.
Typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, sound in air 330 m/s.
A person's speed depends on age, fitness, terrain and distance travelled.
Convert to metres and seconds before calculating.

questions.question: What is the typical speed of a person walking?
questions.explanation: Walking speed is about 1.5 m/s: about one and a half metres every second. 15 m/s is faster than an Olympic sprinter.

questions.question: Which equation correctly links distance travelled (s), speed (v) and time (t)?
questions.explanation: Distance = speed × time. The other forms are incorrect rearrangements.

questions.question: What is a typical speed of sound in air?
questions.explanation: A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. It varies with conditions such as temperature.

questions.question: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Speed has magnitude but no direction. The other three are vectors.

questions.question: Which is closest to the typical speed of a person cycling?
questions.explanation: Cycling speed is about 6 m/s (around 13 mph). 16 m/s would be a fast car in town.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT normally affect how fast a person can run?
questions.explanation: Age, fitness, terrain and distance travelled all affect speed. Clothing colour has no effect.

questions.question:
A car travels at 90 km/h.
What is this speed in m/s?
questions.explanation: 90 × 1000 ÷ 3600 = 25 m/s. 324 comes from multiplying by 3.6 instead of dividing; 1.5 comes from dividing by 60 only.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a toy car on a track.
A student uses a stopwatch to time the toy car between the start line and the finish line.
Why would using light gates give a more accurate time?
options: Light gates make the car go at a constant speed
Light gates remove the effect of human reaction time
Light gates measure the distance more precisely
Light gates reduce friction on the car
questions.explanation: Starting and stopping a stopwatch involves reaction time, which is a large fraction of a short time. Light gates trigger automatically.

questions.question:
A runner runs and then walks.
Table 1 shows information about the two parts of the journey.
What is the average speed for the whole 800 m?
questions.explanation: Time running = 400 ÷ 8.0 = 50 s; time walking = 400 ÷ 2.0 = 200 s. Average speed = 800 ÷ 250 = 3.2 m/s. 5.0 m/s is the trap of averaging the speeds; more time is spent walking, so the average is closer to 2.0 m/s.

questions.question:
A dog runs 60 m in 8.0 s.
Calculate the average speed of the dog.
questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 60 ÷ 8.0 = 7.5 m/s.

questions.question:
A bus travels at a constant speed of 12 m/s for 50 s.
Calculate the distance the bus travels.

A woman walks at 1.5 m/s for 25 minutes.
Calculate the distance she walks in metres.
questions.explanation: Convert minutes to seconds first: 25 × 60 = 1500 s. Then s = v t = 1.5 × 1500 = 2250 m.

questions.question:
A cyclist travels at 6.0 m/s.
Calculate the time taken for the cyclist to travel 3.6 km.
Give your answer in seconds.
questions.explanation: Rearrange s = v t to t = s ÷ v. Convert km to m: 3.6 km = 3600 m. t = 3600 ÷ 6.0 = 600 s (10 minutes).

questions.question:
A train travels at 108 km/h.
Calculate this speed in m/s.

Figure 1 shows a girl watching a storm.
The girl hears the thunder 4.0 s after she sees the lightning flash.
The speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
Calculate the distance between the girl and the lightning.
questions.explanation: Light arrives almost instantly, so the delay is the time for the sound. s = v t = 330 × 4.0 = 1320 m (about 1.3 km).

questions.question:
A car makes a journey in two parts.
Table 1 shows information about the journey.
Calculate the average speed of the car for the whole journey in m/s.
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 15 000 ÷ 900 = 16.7 m/s. Averaging the two separate speeds (25 m/s and 7.1 m/s) gives the wrong answer because the times are different.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a student standing in front of a tall wall.
The student claps once and hears an echo from the wall.
The speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
Calculate the time between the clap and the student hearing the echo.
markScheme: 1 mark: distance travelled by sound = 2 × 99 = 198 m
questions.explanation: The sound must travel to the wall and back, a distance of 198 m. t = 198 ÷ 330 = 0.60 s. Using 99 m gives 0.30 s, which forgets the return trip.

questions.question: Give the SI unit of speed.
questions.explanation: Speed is distance (m) divided by time (s).

questions.question: Give two factors that affect the speed at which a person can walk.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: age, fitness, terrain (type of ground or slope), distance travelled
questions.explanation: AQA lists age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled as factors affecting a person's speed.

questions.question: Give a typical speed for a person running.
questions.explanation: A typical running speed is about 3 m/s, twice walking speed.

questions.question: Explain why the speed calculated from a whole car journey is called an average speed.
markScheme: 1 mark: the car's speed changes / is not constant during the journey (for example slowing at junctions)
1 mark: so total distance ÷ total time gives a single average value, not the speed at every moment
questions.explanation: Real vehicles rarely travel at constant speed, so the calculation gives the average.

questions.question: The speed of sound is often quoted as 330 m/s. Suggest why the speed of sound measured in an experiment might not be exactly 330 m/s.
markScheme: 1 mark: the speed of sound varies with conditions, for example air temperature
1 mark: errors in measuring time, for example human reaction time, or distance
questions.explanation: 330 m/s is a typical value. The real value depends on the air, and timing errors are large when times are short.

questions.question: Describe how a student could measure the average walking speed of a classmate in the school playground.
acceptedAnswers: measure a distance with a tape measure or trundle wheel
markScheme: 1 mark: measure a known distance (for example 20 m) with a tape measure or trundle wheel
1 mark: time the classmate walking the distance with a stopwatch
1 mark: calculate speed = distance ÷ time (repeat and take a mean)
questions.explanation: This is the standard method: known distance, measured time, then speed = distance ÷ time.

questions.question:
A student walks 2 km to school.
Estimate the time taken for the student to walk to school.
Give your answer in minutes.
Show your reasoning.
markScheme: 1 mark: uses a typical walking speed of about 1.5 m/s
questions.explanation: Estimation questions expect you to use the typical speeds you have learned. 2000 ÷ 1.5 = 1333 s, which is about 22 minutes.

questions.question: Compare the typical speeds of walking, running and cycling, and explain why the speed of a person running can change during a long race.
markScheme: Running about 3 m/s, about twice walking speed
Cycling about 6 m/s, about twice running speed and four times walking speed
Speed changes in a race because of fitness / tiredness over long distance
Terrain changes, for example hills or muddy ground slow the runner
Age and fitness of the runner affect the speed they can keep up
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct typical values compared, with at least two reasons for changing speed
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct values or a reason
questions.explanation: AQA expects you to recall the typical speeds and the factors (age, terrain, fitness, distance) that affect them.

questions.question:
Two students want to measure the speed of sound in air.
Figure 1 shows the students on a long, straight, open field.
They have a starting pistol, which makes a flash and a bang, and a stopwatch.
Describe a method the students could use.
Explain how they would calculate the speed of sound and how they could make their result more accurate.
markScheme: Measure a large distance between the students, for example 400 m to 500 m, with a trundle wheel or measuring tape
Student A fires the pistol; student B starts the stopwatch on seeing the flash
Student B stops the stopwatch on hearing the bang
Light travels so fast that its travel time is negligible
Speed of sound = distance ÷ time (expected result about 330 m/s)
Use a large distance so the time is longer and reaction time is a smaller fraction of it
Repeat several times and calculate a mean; discard anomalous results
Swap positions to cancel the effect of wind
